Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This is a very strong paper; rationale and approach are well motivated and carried out.

Some issues came to mind.

1. Eye movements.

There is a clear relationship between eye movements and pupil dilation (e.g. https://peerj.com/articles/1150/). This is not only the case for large saccades but likely for fixational eye movements (FEM) too. Both are likely present during the recording. I wondered, could the authors extract time series of gaze position and use these as a control analysis instead of the pupil time series? Does pupil dilation vary with gaze direction eccentricity? Does gaze direction relate to brain oscillations too or not at all. I guess a simple check is to plot the x-y- ET data together with pupil diameter locked to saccade (both micro and macro) onset. Next, one could re-do the main analysis (e.g. Figure 2 and 5) on data segments pre movement vs. post movement followed by equivalence test or something.

In particular, the anterior δ-theta effects and the visual α could be interpreted within the context of eye movements too. In fact, this could be the one of the "independent mechanisms" the authors speculate about on p. 6 line 216. The authors note that the effect in the visual cortices had the shortest lag with respect to pupil dilation. Yet, visual areas are early in the hierarchy of areas controlling and noticing eye movement. For example if one considers the observations that, cooling of V1 silences cell firing in the superior colliculus (i.e. extended work by Peter Shiller) and in turn eye movement, or some recent work on motor fields in V1 (https://science.sciencemag.org/content/370/6521/1191).

2. MEG gradiometer vs. magnetometer

Is there a difference in the correlation maps between the magnetometer and gradiometer data? A supplemental figure would help here. Basically Figure 4D split by side? Also, is the spectral exponent different for different sensor types? Magnetometers would be likely noisier hence a different aperiodic activity pattern may arise. If so does this impact the pooled results?

From Figure 2B it seems that the data was converted to planar gradient, if so it needs to be mentioned in the methods.

Were head movements monitored and accounted for? Particularly in the context of the data harmonization it would be informative for the reader in the method section. To be clear, the fact that the authors do find effects even if not corrected for head movements speaks for itself. Yet, this is an ongoing debate in MEG research and needs to be mentioned.

3. Pupil data. I was confused what the pupil data actually is. From p. 5 line 164 I understood that cross-correlations were computed between sensor level power and pupil (power? or size?). Later on in Methods the exponent of pupil power spectra is mentioned. All Figures suggest pupil size as indicated by the eye cartoon. Please specify what data (size, power, exponent) is used in which of the different analyses. E.g. Figure 6A is this a correlation between spectral exponent(brain) vs. spectral exponent (pupil)? Do the main results replicate if one uses the absolute pupil size?

RE: The E/I idea. Figure 6 implies then that the whole cortex is a state of excitation which by itself appears in contrast with functional specificity of the E/I idea. In fact, a bit against the authors interpretation on line 441 "modulations of specific cortical oscillations by arousal". All examined band widths and 1/f exponent relate to arousal. The "specificity" argument needs clarification.

Furthermore, I wonder to what extend the same is true if the authors redo the analysis on the planar gradient data? Can the beamformer weakness in modeling deep sources manifest in noise consistency which in turn is captured by the exponent correlation bit?

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The following points relate to points in the public review

#1 spectral analyses. The two analysis types are:

Line 745 – "MEG spectral analysis (all sites)", describes a Morlet wavelet analyses which appears to be used for the results in figures 1-4.

Line 325 and 817 – "Nonlinear relations between pupil-linked arousal and band-limited cortical activity", describes a two second sliding window pwelch analysis.

The sliding window Welch's method analysis will have the same temporal resolution for each frequency band, and the pupil dynamics are matched to the sliding windows used for the MEG. I would strongly suggest running both analyses with Welch's periodogram across sliding windows. This would ensure that dynamics in all frequency have the same resolution and that all analyses in the paper are matched. If there is an additional concern that successive window are independent for the polynomial modelling then the window overlap could be adjusted between the two sections (though independent windows is potentially desirable for the first analysis as well?)

#2 An additional control analysis exploring whether the spatial correlation maps in are associated with source power in the presented frequencies. For example, figure 5D shows the spatial map of the quadratic coefficient at 11 and 19Hz – how closly related is this topography to the simpler spatial distribution of 11Hz and 19Hz power?

#3 From the discussion in Gao et al.,: “Hence, we propose that slope changes in a particular frequency region (30-70 Hz) correspond to changes in E:I balance, while making no claims about other frequency regions”. Not sure what to recommend about the frequency range difference here – at the least it should be acknowledged and discussed. Ideally this analysis should be matched to Gao et al., given how critical this reference is to the discussion and interpretation.

Additional points

#4 It isn't clear where the three frequency bands of interest (line 188: 2-4Hz, 8-16Hz, and 64-128Hz) come from. I think this is based on Figure 1 but only the Glasgow site appears to show distinct clusters in these bands. Hamburg and Munster are significant across the whole 2-32Hz range and Hamburg is additionally significant from 32-128Hz. On this basis, the exclusion of the 4-8Hz and 16-64Hz range seems a bit odd. Some additional clarification and justification would be helpful – apologies if I have missed this in another section.

#5 related to 4, subjectively the MI spectra across the three sites don't seem to be all that similar, a stronger justification for combining subjects in subsequent analyses would be reassuring. Given that this is the jumping off point for the rest of the paper it would be good to revisit this figure to emphasise the points of similarity – the supporting spectra in supplemental materials and topos show between site similarity more convincingly.

To formalise this, can you repeat the between subject correlation matrix from figure S1B for the MI spectra and see if there is substantial banding per-site? if site-specific bands are visible here, then a mixed-modelling approach or the inclusion of a site-covariate in subsequent analyses would be desirable.

results.result: The study pooled MEG and pupil recordings from 81 participants across three laboratories (Glasgow, Hamburg, Münster) under controlled resting-state conditions with constant illumination and sound attenuation. Control analyses confirmed high comparability between laboratories despite differences in setups and participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C225 provide comprehensive methodological details about participant recruitment, ethical approvals, recording procedures, and quality control across all three sites. The control analyses (C42) and supplementary figures demonstrate that recordings were comparable between laboratories, supporting the validity of pooling data.

results.result: Mutual information analysis revealed widespread pupil-brain associations across frequencies with prominent peaks in the 8-32 Hz range, and significant relationships in low-frequency (4-8 Hz) and high-frequency (64-128 Hz) bands across all three datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are directly supported by data in Figure 2A and 2B, showing consistent patterns across all three laboratories. The use of mutual information is appropriate for detecting both monotonic and non-monotonic associations (C45), and the results are statistically significant after FDR correction.

results.result: Control analysis showed that microsaccades caused transient suppression of cortical activity in the 8-32 Hz range but were not associated with changes in pupil diameter.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by control analysis data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. This demonstrates that the observed pupil-brain coupling is not confounded by microsaccade-related artifacts, strengthening the interpretation that effects reflect arousal-related modulation.

results.result: Cross-correlation analysis revealed frequency-dependent temporal lags between pupil diameter and cortical activity: low-frequency (2-4 Hz) activity peaked at 832 ms lag (negative), high-frequency (64-128 Hz) at 562 ms lag (positive), and intermediate frequency (8-16 Hz) at 210 ms lag (positive), with spatially distinct patterns across cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 are well-supported by Figure 3 data showing consistent lag patterns across laboratories. The temporal precedence of cortical activity relative to pupil changes is consistent with known physiology of the arousal system (C51-C53). However, the interpretation relies on assumptions about the relationship between LC/BF activity and pupil diameter based on rodent studies.

results.result: The observed lags between pupil diameter fluctuations and cortical activity are consistent with previously reported lags between noradrenergic/cholinergic activity and pupil diameter in rodents, suggesting different neuromodulatory systems may mediate correlations in different frequency bands.
results.evaluation: While claims C62-C64 compare findings to rodent studies (C121-C122), the interpretation that different neuromodulatory systems drive different frequency bands is speculative. The study did not directly measure neuromodulator activity, and cross-species comparisons have limitations. The evidence is suggestive but not definitive.

results.result: Source-level analysis revealed frequency-dependent and region-specific correlations between pupil diameter and cortical activity: negative correlations with low-frequency (2-8 Hz) activity were widespread, while intermediate (8-32 Hz) and high-frequency (>50 Hz) activity showed spatially heterogeneous patterns with opposite signs across different cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C81 are well-supported by Figure 4 data showing detailed spatial and spectral patterns. The source reconstruction methods are appropriate, and the findings demonstrate region-specific effects that challenge the view of arousal as a global, uniform modulator. Statistical significance is established with FDR correction.

results.result: Analysis of pupil derivative yielded largely similar spatial patterns to pupil diameter but with reduced correlation magnitudes, consistent with previous rodent studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are supported by supplementary figure data and comparison to McGinley et al., 2015a. This provides additional validation that the observed effects are related to arousal rather than artifacts, though the weaker magnitudes suggest pupil diameter may be a more sensitive measure in this context.

results.result: Nonlinear analysis revealed an inverted U-shaped relationship between pupil-linked arousal and cortical activity specifically in the alpha/beta frequency band (8-32 Hz) and parieto-occipital cortices, with activity maximal at intermediate pupil diameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 are supported by Figure 5 data showing quadratic relationships. The polynomial fitting approach is appropriate, and the inverted U pattern is statistically significant and spatially specific. This finding extends previous rodent work (C162) to humans and identifies a novel frequency-specific nonlinearity.

results.result: The spectral exponent of the aperiodic component decreased linearly with pupil diameter across 92.5% of brain regions, suggesting widespread arousal-related changes in cortical excitation-inhibition balance, with notable exceptions in extrastriate occipital cortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C109 are supported by Figure 6A-C data. The widespread negative correlation between spectral exponent and pupil diameter is robust and statistically significant. However, the interpretation that this reflects E/I balance (C11, C99, C178) relies on computational modeling and optogenetic studies in mice (C101-C102), which may not directly translate to human MEG recordings.

results.result: Control analysis removing the aperiodic component confirmed that pupil-brain coupling with band-limited activity represents genuine arousal-related modulation of periodic cortical activity rather than spurious correlations induced by changes in the aperiodic component.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 are supported by Figure 6D control analysis. The pattern of correlations remained largely unchanged after removing the aperiodic component, confirming that the frequency-specific effects are not artifacts of spectral slope changes. This is an important methodological validation.

results.result: The study's findings are consistent with previous rodent and primate studies showing that elevated arousal is accompanied by decreased low-frequency and increased high-frequency activity, with temporal lags comparable to those reported between LC activation and pupil dilation.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C123 appropriately contextualize findings within existing literature. The consistency with rodent studies (C22-C23) and primate work (C120) supports the validity of the results. However, the interpretation that different neuromodulatory systems drive different frequency bands remains speculative without direct measurement of neuromodulator activity.

results.result: The short-lag positive correlation in visual cortices may stem from LC-thalamus interactions affecting thalamo-cortical feedback loops involved in alpha-band activity generation, potentially mediated by noradrenergic or cholinergic modulation, or by GABAergic LC neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 propose mechanistic explanations for the observed short-lag effects in visual cortex, but these are speculative hypotheses based on anatomical knowledge and prior studies. The study did not directly test these mechanisms, and alternative explanations are possible. Further experimental work would be needed to validate these interpretations.

results.result: The positive correlation between tonic pupil size and alpha activity in visual cortex during rest does not contradict previous findings of negative correlations with phasic pupil responses during tasks, due to the inverse relationship between tonic and phasic pupil responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C135 provide a coherent explanation for apparent discrepancies with prior task-based studies. The distinction between tonic and phasic pupil responses is well-established (C132), and the agreement with Whitmarsh et al., 2021 (C135) supports this interpretation. This demonstrates careful consideration of the literature.

results.result: The temporal cascade of arousal effects may represent routine 'monitoring sweeps' during mind-wandering, involving cessation of synchronized low-frequency activity, increased high-frequency activity for sensory processing, modulation of hippocampal theta related to memory retrieval, and return to synchronized alpha/beta activity marking shift to introspective focus.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C155 propose an integrative functional interpretation of the temporal cascade, but this is largely speculative. While individual components are supported by data (e.g., hippocampal theta correlations C147) and prior literature (C146, C148-C150, C153-C154), the overall narrative of 'monitoring sweeps' is a hypothesis that requires direct testing with behavioral measures or task manipulations.

results.result: The inverted U-shaped relationship between arousal and alpha/beta activity may result from differential activation of noradrenergic receptor subtypes, with high-affinity α2 receptors activated at medium arousal levels and low-affinity α1 receptors at elevated arousal.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C168 propose a receptor-based mechanism for the inverted U relationship, but this is speculative. While the differential receptor hypothesis is plausible based on prior work (C166), the study did not measure receptor activation or manipulate receptor subtypes. This interpretation requires pharmacological validation.

results.result: The coexistence of monotonic and inverted U relationships between arousal and alpha/beta activity in overlapping cortical regions may reflect distinct influences on separate alpha rhythm generators with different functional roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C173 propose that spatially overlapping effects reflect distinct alpha rhythms, supported by prior evidence for multiple alpha generators (C172). However, the study did not directly separate or characterize distinct alpha rhythms, making this interpretation speculative. Further analysis would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: The negative correlation between pupil diameter and spectral exponent suggests that increased arousal co-occurs with increased excitation-inhibition ratio in distributed cortical circuits, consistent with noradrenergic effects on cortical E/I.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C180 interpret spectral exponent changes as reflecting E/I balance based on computational models (C177) and prior pharmacological studies (C179). However, the link between spectral exponent and E/I in human MEG is indirect and relies on cross-species extrapolation. The interpretation is plausible but requires validation with more direct measures of E/I balance.

results.result: The diverse relationships between pupil-linked arousal and cortical activity challenge the view of arousal as a global, uniform modulator and support region-specific, frequency-specific, and temporally-varying neuromodulatory influences that should be considered as covariates in future studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C189 provide appropriate synthesis of the study's implications. The data clearly demonstrate spatial, spectral, and temporal heterogeneity in arousal effects, challenging traditional views (C3, C16-C17). The recommendation to include arousal as a covariate in future studies is well-justified by the findings and agreement with independent work (C186).

results.result: The study identified a cascade of arousal effects: decreases in low-frequency (2-8 Hz) activity in temporal and lateral frontal cortex, followed by increased high-frequency (>64 Hz) activity in mid-frontal regions, followed by monotonic and inverted U relationships with intermediate frequency (8-32 Hz) activity in occipito-parietal regions, along with widespread changes in aperiodic activity indicative of excitation-inhibition balance changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 and C33-C36 summarize the main findings, which are well-supported by the data presented in Figures 2-6. The cascade of effects is demonstrated through cross-correlation analysis (Figure 3), the spatial patterns are shown in source-level analysis (Figure 4), the nonlinear relationships are established through polynomial fitting (Figure 5), and the aperiodic changes are documented (Figure 6). These represent the core novel contributions of the study.
